title: The Tell-Tale Heart
author: Edgar Allan Poe
summary: Um homem jura que não é louco e conta sua história para provar isso. Ele mora com um velho bondoso, mas não suporta um dos olhos dele, pálido e frio como o de um abutre. Noite após noite, ele entra no quarto escuro do velho, em silêncio, com uma lanterna na mão. É um conto de suspense sombrio, cheio de medo, culpa e sons no escuro.

chapters.title: The Eye
paragraphs: True! I am nervous. I am very, very nervous. But why do you say I am mad? I am not mad. My senses are sharp. My ears are very good. I hear everything in heaven and on earth. I hear many things in hell too. So how can I be mad? Listen. I can tell you the whole story calmly.
I live in a house with an old man. I love the old man. He is kind to me. He never hurts me. He never says bad things to me. I do not want his money. I do not want his gold.

So what is the problem? It is his eye. Yes, it is his eye! One of his eyes is like the eye of a vulture. It is pale blue, with a thin film over it. When the eye looks at me, my blood goes cold. I hate it. I cannot live with it.
Slowly, day by day, an idea comes into my head. I must kill the old man. Then I can close that eye forever.
Now you think I am mad. But mad men are stupid. Mad men know nothing. Look at me! I am careful. I am clever. I plan everything. You must see how wisely I work!

chapters.title: Seven Nights
paragraphs: Every day, I am very kind to the old man. I smile at him. I talk to him nicely. He has no idea of my plan.

Every night, at about midnight, I go to his room. I turn the handle of his door very slowly. I open the door very, very slowly. It takes me one hour! I put my head into the room. I have a lantern in my hand. It is closed, so there is no light.

Then I open the lantern a little bit. Only one thin ray of light comes out. I put the light on the vulture eye. But every night the eye is closed. So I cannot do the work. It is not the old man I hate. It is his Evil Eye.
In the morning, I go into his room with a happy face. “Good morning!” I say. “How are you? Did you sleep well?” He does not suspect anything.
I do this for seven long nights. Seven nights at midnight. And seven nights the eye is closed.

On the eighth night, I am even more careful. The hand of a clock moves faster than my hand. I feel so strong! I feel so clever! The old man is in his bed. He is dreaming. He does not know about me, outside his door. I almost laugh at the idea.

Then I move a little, and he moves too. Maybe he hears me. I do not go back. The room is black, black as tar. The old man is afraid of robbers, so the windows are shut. I know he cannot see the door. So I push it, slowly, slowly.

chapters.title: The Eighth Night
paragraphs: My head is in the room. I want to open the lantern. But my thumb slips on the metal. It makes a small noise.
The old man jumps up in his bed. “Who's there?” he cries.

I do not move. I do not make a sound. For one whole hour I stand there, like a statue. He does not lie down again. He is sitting up in the bed, listening. I know how he feels. I am often awake at night like him, full of terror.

Then I hear a little groan. It is a groan of fear, not of pain. I know that sound. The old man is afraid. He is saying to himself, “It is nothing. It is only the wind. It is only a mouse.” But he knows it is not true. Death is in the room with him.
I wait a long time. Then I open the lantern a little. A thin ray of light goes out, like the thread of a spider. It falls on the vulture eye.
The eye is open! It is wide, wide open. I see it clearly. It is dull blue, with that horrible film. It makes me cold to my bones.
Then I hear a sound. It is low and quick, like a watch inside cotton. I know that sound too. It is the beating of the old man's heart! It makes me angry, like a drum makes a soldier brave.
The beating gets faster and louder. Louder! Louder! Maybe the neighbours can hear it! The old man's hour is here.

I shout and jump into the room. He screams once, only once. I pull him to the floor. I pull the heavy bed over him. I smile. The work is done. For many minutes, the heart beats with a soft sound. Then it stops. The old man is dead. His eye can never trouble me again.

chapters.title: Visitors at Four O'Clock
paragraphs: Do you still think I am mad? Then listen to the next part. I work quickly, but in silence. I hide the body. I take up three boards from the floor of the room. I put everything under them. Then I put the boards back, very carefully. No human eye can see anything wrong. Not even his eye! There is no blood. There is nothing to wash. I am too clever for that.
At four o'clock the work is finished. It is still dark outside. Then someone knocks at the street door. I go down with a light heart. What is there to fear now?
Three men are at the door. They are police officers. They are very polite. “A neighbour heard a scream in the night,” says one officer. “We must search the house.”
I smile. “Come in, gentlemen,” I say. “The scream is mine. I had a bad dream. The old man is not here. He is visiting friends in the country.”
I take them all over the house. “Search everything,” I say. “Search well.” I show them his money and his gold. Nothing is missing.
Then I take them into his room. I bring chairs. “Please sit down and rest,” I say. I feel so confident. I put my own chair right over the boards. Right over the body!
The officers are happy. My answers are calm and easy. They sit and talk with me about ordinary things. I talk and laugh with them.

chapters.title: The Sound
paragraphs: But soon I feel pale. I want the men to go. My head hurts. There is a ringing in my ears. The men are still sitting and talking.
The ringing gets clearer. I talk more and more, to stop the feeling. But it does not stop. Then I understand. The noise is not in my ears.
It is a low, quick sound. It is like a watch inside cotton. I know that sound! I breathe fast. I talk faster and louder. But the noise gets louder too.

I stand up. I argue about little things in a high voice. I wave my hands. The noise gets louder. I walk up and down the room with heavy steps. The noise gets louder! Oh God! What can I do? I swing my chair. I scrape it on the boards. But the noise is louder than everything. Louder! Louder! Louder!
And the men? They are still talking and smiling. Can they not hear it? Oh, yes! They hear it! They know! They are laughing at me! They are playing with my terror! I am sure of it.
Anything is better than this pain. Anything is better than their smiles. I must scream or die! And now, again, listen! Louder! Louder! Louder! LOUDER!
“Villains!” I scream. “Stop pretending! I did it! Pull up the boards! Here, here! It is the beating of his hideous heart!”
